text: @snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite 为 DSH 提供可配置的 LLM 服务商适配层，可在一份配置中声明多个服务商端点及其模型目录，并将模型路由注册到 Harness 的 LLM 服务。它支持 OpenAI Chat Completions、Anthropic Messages 和 OpenAI Responses 三种接口，按模型声明转换对话、工具调用、推理内容与流式响应。Web 设置页面可编辑服务商和模型、保存凭据并查询端点模型。适合需要连接兼容接口或自建模型网关的 DSH 部署；需配置服务商端点，凭据按配置选择。

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite connects custom LLM providers to DSH. Configure endpoint profiles and model catalogs for OpenAI Chat Completions, Anthropic Messages, or OpenAI Responses. Its web settings support provider editing, credential storage, and endpoint model discovery.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite 的功能「多协议服务商路由」：按服务商配置选择 Chat Completions、Anthropic Messages 或 Responses 接口，并将模型请求转发到对应端点。
@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite 的功能「服务商与模型档案」：为每个服务商声明端点、协议和模型能力，再将可用档案注册为 DSH LLM 路由。
@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite 的功能「端点模型发现」：在配置时向兼容端点查询模型清单，并将返回结果交给设置界面展示以辅助编辑。
@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite 的功能「Web 模型配置」：在 Plugins 配置页和 Models 页面编辑同一份服务商配置，并提供凭据保存与模型发现操作。
@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite 使用时需配置服务商端点；模型请求会发往所选端点，具体 API 凭据由服务商配置决定。

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Mount：The package declares itself a bundle (`dsh.bundle.patch`), so the install above
also mounts its `llm-service-lite` row: one command installs and mounts, and no
hand-written entry is needed. The mount is dormant — no route exists until a
profile declares one.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Mount：Two surfaces edit the same document. In the web UI, open **Plugins**, select
this bundle, open its `llm-service-lite` row, and choose **Configure**: the
page lists every provider, adds and removes profiles, edits the endpoint,
protocol, capabilities and model catalog, stores an API key through the
harness credential service, and asks an endpoint which models it serves. The
same document can be edited by hand in the profile's own `cordis.patch.yml`
(`$DSH_HOME/profiles/<profile>/cordis.patch.yml`; **Settings → Open
configuration file** in the web UI opens it). Add the `providers` dictionary
described under [Configure provider profiles](#configure-provider-profiles) to
the `llm-service-lite` row's `config`. The profile patch is applied after every
bundle layer, so that entry's `config` replaces the row's empty default; the
same entry also mounts the plugin in a composition that declares no bundle
layer, because it names the module to load:

- id: llm-service-lite
  name: '@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite'
  config:
    providers:

After the install, refresh the Web page once: the browser half is served by
the client module system, so the new page appears on the **Plugins** screen the
next time the shell boots. It lives on the bundle's page and on its
`llm-service-lite` row, where that row's **Configure** control opens it.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Mount：The plugin fills the **Models** page's adapter-family extension seats while the
Host serves its settings namespace: every `llm-service-lite` provider card gets
the plugin's own editor, and the section footer gets the same add-provider
builder. The builder asks for a preset, route, protocol, endpoint, optional key,
and runs a connection test before writing; the editor covers protocol, endpoint,
credential, request behavior, a connection test, and the model catalog. The
catalog is a filterable list with one expanded model editor; effort levels and
thinking modes are localized toggles, and **Fill capabilities** applies the
documented family defaults to fields a model left open. `extraBody` sits behind
an advanced disclosure and blocks a save when its JSON is malformed. The plugin's
page on the **Plugins** screen edits the same row `config`. Hand-written fields it does not
render (`headers`, `imageTokens`, `imagePixelBudget`, `imageMaxBytes`, `catalog`,
`retryPolicy`, and the per-model `defaults`) are preserved by every save and
remain editable in the patch.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Mount：Credentials are named, not inlined, in a managed profile: set `apiKeyEnv` to the
reference (`DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`, say) and store the secret through the harness
credential service, export it in the launching environment, or keep it in the
harness home's `.env`. The reference is resolved on every request, and a named
reference that resolves to nothing fails the request with `MISSING_CREDENTIAL`
instead of sending it unauthenticated. A profile imported verbatim from OWCode
may keep its inline `apiKey`.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Mount：Mount it exactly once. When a composition already carries an `llm-service-lite`
row (the archived [dsh-lite](https://github.com/snnh/dsh-lite) fork's `dsh-base`
bundle shipped one), that row already reaches this package: install without
activating it as a bundle — `dsh plugin --profile web add -D
@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite` — and configure the existing row. Keep exactly one
layer for the row: a later layer's same-id insert replaces the earlier row and
its **whole `config`** — patch layers never deep-merge — so a second row
silently discards what the first configured; it does not mount a second
instance.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Route names：Route names must be unique across the adapters mounted in one composition. On
stock upstream profiles the shipped `llm-pi-ai` catalog already declares common
provider names (`deepseek`, `openai`, `anthropic`, and similar), so prefer a
distinct route id that names the endpoint itself — `deepseek-direct`,
`company-gateway` — rather than a name an installed catalog may own. A profile
whose route name another adapter already owns is skipped with one warning naming
the owner instead of failing the mount, the rest of the profiles register, and a
newly written profile that claims such a name is refused where it is written;
renaming its route is the repair. The plugin also refuses, by name, the routes
the first-party DeepSeek channel owns; see [Use this package](#use-this-package).

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Compatibility：This package drives the public seam of `@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm` and the
`@deepseek-ai/cordis` service layer, so it runs against a published harness
rather than a checkout: its peers are the harness packages, and the profile
that loads it already owns the copies the runtime uses. The development
baseline is harness `0.2.1-rc.2` — `devDependencies` pin those packages and the
test suite runs against them — while the `^0.2.1-alpha.2` peer ranges also admit
the `0.2.1` alpha line, so an older `0.2.1` harness loads the same package.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Compatibility：Two declarations of the archived [dsh-lite](https://github.com/snnh/dsh-lite)
fork are used when the running harness carries them and skipped when it does
not: the model-defaults registration seam a configuration surface asks for
declared model ids, and the `outputModalities` field on a model's info. Upstream
`0.2.1-rc.2` carries neither, so both are inert there: the adapter keeps its
family defaults on the request path, where they still fill the fields a profile
left open, and the extra field is simply ignored by the runtime.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Summary：`@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite` adapts third-party model endpoints: one route per configured provider profile, all answered over its transports — the OpenAI-compatible chat-completions wire, the Anthropic Messages protocol, and the OpenAI Responses API — so no provider SDK and no installed catalog sits in the request path. A profile is self-contained — wire protocol, endpoint, credential reference, request-body extras, concurrency, image input, and the models served — so a gateway, a national API, and a corporate proxy reach one code path. The shape ports OpenWebCode's model-provider layer onto the harness seam: one document describes every provider, and the route set follows it live.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Use this package：Mount this plugin when a deployment wants to describe its model providers itself instead of naming providers an installed catalog already knows. The `providers` dictionary is the whole configuration surface: each key is the provider route a request selects with `GenerateOptions.provider`, and the value is everything that endpoint needs.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · When to choose it：This plugin adapts third-party endpoints and nothing else: every route it registers comes from a profile a deployment wrote, and the first-party DeepSeek channel keeps its own adapter. DeepSeek is that channel by default, so the route names it owns — `deepseek-official` and `deepseek-account`, registered by `@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm-deepseek-api-key` and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm-deepseek-account` — are refused here by name, with the owner in the diagnostic, rather than claimed and left to fail plugin loading. DeepSeek itself keeps those modules — this adapter is not a substitute for that channel. Any other route name is free: a deployment that reaches a DeepSeek-compatible endpoint through this adapter names its own route and declares that endpoint's own capabilities. Choose this adapter when the same composition serves several endpoints — a national model API, a self-hosted vLLM or SGLang gateway, and a proxy on the corporate network — and each must be described completely rather than derived from a catalog. @snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Start from an official configuration file：An official deployment publishes one provider file per provider — an API-keyed map of `chat:` entries. `catalog` converts such a file into this adapter's own vocabulary: the API becomes the route's `interfaceType` (`openai-completions` to `openai-chat-completions`, `openai-responses`, `anthropic-messages`), `baseUrl` becomes `baseURL`, a header set every model shares becomes the route's headers, and each chat entry becomes a model with its id, name, `contextWindow`, `maxTokens`, input modalities, and thinking levels. A model's `samplingParams` become its `defaults`, so an endpoint's own sampling settings arrive as configuration rather than as a caller concern. Fields this adapter has no counterpart for — `cost`, `compat` flags it does not model, `inputLimits`, and model types it does not serve — are reported one line each instead of guessed, and the route still serves. A header set every entry shares becomes the route's `headers`; only header sets that disagree, which one route cannot carry, are reported. text: @snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Declare what a model can do：A model entry's `capabilities` are declarations about the endpoint, never guesses: a capability left out is one this adapter does not claim, and one it declares is honoured or refused by name — never accepted with nothing behind it. `effort` lists the selectable reasoning levels and its values are the wire spellings, so a gateway with its own vocabulary declares that vocabulary. `thinking` lists the accepted thinking modes (`enabled`, `disabled`, `adaptive`). `thinkingStyle` says how the endpoint spells the switch: `thinking: { type: … }`, a top-level `enable_thinking` boolean, `fixed` for a model that always thinks, or `effort_only` — the explicit spelling of an endpoint that takes an effort level and has no switch, which is the same request an omitted style sends. `reasoningContent` declares that the endpoint returns reasoning in `reasoning_content`, which is what lets a later request replay prior thinking. `replayReasoning` decides whether that prior thinking actually travels back: absent defers to the model's family (see below), `true` sends it, and a family whose follow-up turns are rejected without it refuses to

text: @snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Declare what a model can do：**Family defaults.** A hand-written profile states what its author knows and leaves the rest to the model's family: `src/model-defaults.ts` is a reviewed table of what the mainstream families document — the image input a vision model takes, the effort ladder and the level its own platform applies by default, the switch spelling, and whether prior reasoning must travel back. The table only fills what the profile left open, so a profile field always wins; a family that shows no entry for a model leaves the adapter's own conservative answer in place; and nothing in it defaults a sampling parameter, because vendors disagree about the reachable ranges and the endpoint's own default beats an invented one. Each entry records the vendor documentation it came from, and only the model owner's own platform is ever a source: what a reseller or gateway requires of the same model id is not.
section: Declare what a model can do

text: @snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Declare what a model can do：A model entry's `defaults` state the request parameters its endpoint wants when the caller states none: `temperature`, `topP`, `topK`, and `maxTokens`. Each is written only where the caller's own request left it unstated, so a default can never override an explicit choice; `topK` is refused on `openai-responses`, which has no top-k field; and `defaults.maxTokens` is what a caller that stated no cap receives. A model's own `maxTokens` is a capacity rather than a request default, and the three transports treat the output cap differently: `chat-completions` sends `max_tokens` only when the caller, or a declared `defaults.maxTokens`, supplied one, so an endpoint that defaults its own ceiling keeps it; `anthropic-messages` requires the field on every request and takes the caller's value, then the profile's `extraBody.max_tokens`, then `defaults.maxTokens`, then the model's family cap, then 64K for a model no family speaks for; `openai-responses` also always sends `max_output_tokens`, from the caller's value, then `defaults.maxTokens`, then the model's `maxTokens` (the route's `defaultMaxTokens` when the model declares none)

text: @snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Change configuration at runtime：Each operation captures the current provider set. A changed route set — or a route's display name or retry policy, which the registry captures at registration — re-registers the same adapter instance in place, so an in-flight request keeps the endpoint it started with and the next request sees the new one. Concurrency is admission-level rather than registration-level: changing `maxConcurrent` updates the route's existing queue on the next request instead of re-registering it, and requests already queued keep their place. A profile that cannot be served is refused where it is written and, when already stored, kept addressable with its diagnostic instead of taking the other routes down with it; a profile whose route name another adapter owns is reported and skipped at mount (see [Route names](#route-names)) instead of aborting the composition.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Discover models from endpoints：The plugin answers "which models can this endpoint serve?" for a route a configuration surface is editing or drafting. A configured route supplies its stored endpoint, protocol, headers, and credential inside the Host; a draft supplies its own endpoint and protocol, and a one-shot key wins over the stored credential for that query. The listing is protocol-aware: the two OpenAI-compatible wires query `GET {baseURL}/models` with bearer auth, an Anthropic Messages route queries that protocol's own `/v1/models` listing with `x-api-key` and `anthropic-version`, and both published OpenAI-compatible shapes are accepted — the standard `data` array and the enriched `models` map. The reply is candidate metadata a surface may offer for adoption: nothing is stored, and the profile a user saves decides what a route serves. An endpoint that cannot be reached, answers without JSON, or sends more than 4 MiB fails the query with `DISCOVERY_FAILED`; an endpoint error status is reported as `INVALID_REQUEST`, and a protocol with no readable listing is refused as `INVALID_CONFIG`.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Failures and recovery：Failures carry stable codes: a named credential that resolves to nothing fails with `MISSING_CREDENTIAL`, a rejected request with `INVALID_REQUEST`, an exhausted quota with `QUOTA` rather than a rate limit, and a request that exceeds the model context with `CONTEXT_WINDOW_EXCEEDED`, which is what lets the agent compact instead of retrying. A stream that ends without a terminal event fails with `TRANSPORT` rather than looking like a finished turn, and a completion that carries no content fails with `EMPTY_RESPONSE`. A provider-requested delay is read from `Retry-After` and handed to the retry layer.
@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Failures and recovery：

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Design philosophy：Three rules shape the package. A profile is the whole truth: nothing is inferred from an installed catalog, so an endpoint that is not OpenAI, Anthropic, or DeepSeek is configured, not special-cased. A declared capability is a promise: the request path sends only what the profile declares and never invents a knob. And a failure is classified where it happens: the transport turns each HTTP status and error body into one stable code, because that is the only point that sees the whole provider answer.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Registration and directory：A mount with no profiles registers nothing: the plugin holds no route until its settings section supplies one, which is why the base bundle can mount it dormant. Every route this instance mounts appears in the configurable-provider directory, including one that is disabled or currently unserviceable, so a settings surface can address and repair it by name. A profile skipped because another mounted adapter already owns its route name stays out of the directory — that name belongs to the other family, and renaming the profile's route is the repair (see [Route names](#route-names)).

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Wire translation：Three transports answer one seam. `openai-chat-completions` speaks the OpenAI-compatible wire and `anthropic-messages` the Messages protocol, and both own the three things a provider stream does not: block identity and ordering, tool-call assembly across streamed fragments, and the difference between a stream that ended and one that was cut off.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Wire translation：Both also repair their protocol's pairing rules on the way out, because a durable history can hold shapes no endpoint accepts. A result whose call is gone is dropped; a call id one assistant turn declares twice, or that a later turn declares again, collapses to its first occurrence; a repeat result for one call is dropped and its first occurrence kept; a call nothing ever answered is answered with a placeholder rather than left to a 400; and the results of one parallel batch merge into the single user turn both protocols require. The repair happens in the wire projection, so the durable log is never rewritten to make a request acceptable.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Wire translation：Reasoning is replayed only for a route whose target model declares it, and only for history the same provider produced. `openai-chat-completions` replays it through `reasoning_content` and matches the history on the provider alone; `anthropic-messages` and `openai-responses` additionally require the source model to match, and replay signed/redacted thinking blocks or the provider's own reasoning items through adapter-private replay metadata on the assistant message. The Messages protocol rejects a thinking block returned without its signature, and metadata another provider, another model, or another adapter wrote degrades that one turn to plain text instead of failing the request.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Wire translation：The Responses transport maps the conversation onto the API's flat item list — an assistant `message`, a `function_call` per call, and a `function_call_output` carrying the same id — and repairs that list the same way, with one difference the protocol forces: a call nothing answered is dropped rather than answered with a placeholder, because strict gateways reject a fabricated output, and a turn's parallel calls are grouped so the API folds them into one assistant turn. Its reasoning follows the model's declaration: `reasoningContent` replays the thinking text as `reasoning_text`, and `responsesEncryptedReplay` hands the provider's own item back verbatim. The protocol carries no stop sequences, so a caller's `stop` is omitted rather than approximated.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Wire translation：The Messages transport reads its prompt from `system`, else from a leading system message. A later system or developer message folds into a user turn where it stands and a mid-conversation instruction keeps its position — unless the model declared `systemPromptUpdate` or `toolUpdate`, in which case that message travels as the `system`-role history message this protocol reserves for mid-history changes, with tool additions and removals spelled as references to the declared tools. Such a message is held back until the turn it follows is a user turn, because the protocol reads it as an instruction between turns, and a change that would land earlier is refused by name rather than moved. Tool results carry their media inline as image blocks beside their text, `max_tokens` is always sent because the protocol requires the cap, and `promptCaching` marks this protocol's own breakpoints: the system prompt and the last tool declaration.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Model Experience：The provider-configuration page under **Plugins** is operator-only: it edits Host configuration and contributes no model-visible prompt, tool, or context surface. The model experience described below is unchanged by the page.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · What the model sees：The conversation exactly as the harness assembled it: the system prompt as a leading system message, user and assistant turns in order, tool declarations as function schemas, and each tool result attached to the call it answers. A request adds the endpoint's own `extraBody` fields and, when the model declares how it spells them, the effort level and thinking switch the caller selected.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Token effect：The request carries no adapter-authored system-prompt text; the only text this adapter itself contributes is deterministic framing — the `Attached media from tool result:` note the two OpenAI wires lead a tool-result media follow-up with, a placeholder for a tool result that never landed, and the `[context trimmed]` marker for a Messages assistant turn that cannot otherwise be carried. `max_tokens` is present on a chat-completions request only when the caller configured one, so an endpoint that defaults its own ceiling keeps it; the Messages and Responses protocols require an output cap, so both always send one — from the request, the profile's `defaults`, or the model's declared cap (Responses raises a value below the API's 16-token floor).

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · KV Cache effect：Nothing in the translation is per-request random: the same history produces the same request bytes, so provider-side prefix caching keeps working across turns. A route marked `promptCaching` uses the protocol's own cache marking — the Messages transport marks the system prompt and the last tool declaration — and otherwise the adapter adds no cache breakpoints of its own.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · What the model sees：Content deltas become text blocks, `reasoning_content` becomes reasoning blocks, signed thinking becomes a reasoning block whose signature is kept as replay metadata, and streamed tool-call fragments become one call each. The model's own stop reason is mapped onto the harness vocabulary, and a stream that ends without one is a transport failure rather than a completed turn.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Token effect：Usage is reported when the endpoint sends it, with cached prompt tokens separated out of the input count exactly as the harness contracts: `inputTokens` excludes what the provider served from cache, which is reported as `cacheReadTokens`.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · KV Cache effect：Replayed reasoning is byte-identical to what the provider returned, so a route that echoes reasoning back keeps its cache prefix stable; a route that does not declare `reasoningContent` sends no reasoning at all rather than a paraphrase.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Development：`tsconfig.test.json` typechecks the specs, which the shipping `tsconfig.json`
does not include; CI runs `pnpm run check` on Node 22 and 24. The package is
plain ESM and bundles only its own code: every harness package stays external,
because the profile that loads the plugin owns the single runtime copy of them.
`build/client-bundle.mjs` wraps the emitted browser half into the client module
system's factory format (`lib/client.js`, the target of the `./client` export),
leaving React and the shared UI packages to the page's frozen module table.

@snnh/dsh-llm-service-lite README · Development：Beyond the runtime entry, the package carries its own declarations:
`cordis.patch.yml` is the bundle layer that mounts the plugin row,
`package.json`'s `dsh.bundle.patch` points at it, and `locale/*.json` plus
`icon.svg` are the display resources a plugin inventory reads without loading
the plugin. `tests/declaration.spec.ts` holds the three together, so keep
`exports` and `files` covering every added asset.
